account: M. D. Keall of the University of Otago in Wellington and S. Newstead of the Monash University Accident Research Centre in Melbourne analyzed injury crashes in Australia and New Zealand from 2016 to 2023. They classed a vehicle as having pedestrian autonomous emergency braking (PAEB) when Redbook vehicle specifications listed pedestrian avoidance with braking, and they used an induced exposure method that controlled for jurisdiction, speed limit, vehicle market group, driver age and sex, weather, light and year. Vehicles with PAEB had a 17% lower rate of pedestrian or cyclist collisions (95% CI 5% to 27%) than vehicles without any AEB. Vehicles with AEB that lacked pedestrian detection showed no reduction in these collisions. Collisions with motorcycles fell 11% with PAEB (95% CI 0% to 21%). The authors estimated that the benefit was higher at night, which differs from some other studies. Traffic Injury Prevention published the study online on 11 June 2026. The design is observational, the fitment data come from specifications, and the data held too few cyclists for a separate cyclist estimate.
